The Dead Sea is called "dead" due to the absence of aquatic life in its waters. This is primarily attributed to its extremely high salinity, which creates an environment inhospitable to most forms of life. The geological and chemical reasons for its extreme salinity involve a combination of geographical features and natural processes. 

The Dead Sea is a landlocked, hypersaline lake located in a rift valley between Jordan and Israel. It has no natural outlet, meaning water can only leave through evaporation. This lack of an outlet causes minerals and salts dissolved in the water to accumulate over time. The primary source of these salts is the inflow of water from rivers such as the Jordan River, which carries dissolved minerals from the surrounding rocks and soil. 

Additionally, the region experiences high temperatures and low rainfall, leading to a high evaporation rate. As water evaporates, it leaves behind the dissolved salts, further increasing the salinity of the remaining water. Over thousands of years, this process has resulted in the Dead Sea having one of the highest salt concentrations in the world, approximately 34% salinity, which is about ten times saltier than the ocean. 

The extreme salinity prevents most aquatic organisms from surviving, as the high concentration of salt disrupts their cellular functions. This lack of life, combined with the inability to support complex ecosystems, has led to the name "Dead Sea."
